title: Seventh Nerve Disorders & Bell's Palsy
summary: A comprehensive clinical guide to the motor, sensory, and secretory functions of the facial nerve, highlighting the critical importance of lid closure in ophthalmology and the evidence-based management of Bell's palsy.

sections.title: Ophthalmic Importance of the VII Nerve
sections.content: The seventh or facial nerve has a number of important motor, sensory, and secretory functions. Of these, it is the facial nerve’s ability to close the eyelids (i.e. innervation of orbicularis oculi) that make it so important to the ophthalmologist. Facial nerve palsy should not be underestimated. Do not automatically assume that every facial nerve palsy is a ‘Bell’s palsy’, and be alert to its capacity to cause blinding exposure keratopathy (see Box 16.15). Anatomy: See E Anatomy and physiology (3), p. 732.

branches: Motor: muscles of facial expression and movement
Motor: superficial platysma muscles of the neck
Sensory/Secretory: lacrimal gland (via greater superficial petrosal nerve)
Sensory: taste for anterior two-thirds of tongue (via chorda tympani)

rows: Weakness of one side of the face/facial asymmetry (if unilateral).
Lagophthalmos, with or without lower lid ectropion.
Check for alteration of taste, salivation, and lacrimation.

sections.title: Differential: UMN vs. LMN Lesions
content: Upper Motor Neurone (UMN): Upper facial muscles still function (e.g. can still raise eyebrows) due to bilateral innervation (see E Anatomy and physiology (3), p. 732).
Lower Motor Neurone (LMN): Both upper and lower facial muscles are involved.

sections.title: Complex Palsy: Cranial Nerve Check
content: Check Vn: Cerebel-lopontine lesions
Check VIn: Lesion in pons
Check VIIn: Cerebellopontine angle lesions

sections.title: Box 16.15: Causes of VIIn Palsy
content: • Bell’s palsy (idiopathic).
• Ramsay–hunt syndrome (varicella-zoster infection).
• Cerebellopontine angle lesions.
• Trauma.
• Otitis.
• Neurofibroma (NF-2).
• Parotid gland mass.
• Congenital (e.g. Moebius’ syndrome).
• Guillain–Barré syndrome (Commonly present with bilateral VIIn weakness).
• Lyme disease (Commonly present with bilateral VIIn weakness).
• Sarcoidosis (Commonly present with bilateral VIIn weakness).
• Meningitis (Commonly present with bilateral VIIn weakness).

sections.title: Bell's Palsy Clinical Data
sections.content: Bell’s palsy (idiopathic facial paralysis) is a diagnosis of exclusion. It can affect any age group (peak 40y), with males and females equally affected. Associations include diabetes and pregnancy. Symptoms reach their peak at 48h; most start recovery at 3wk.

sections.title: Management Strategy: New & Recurrent Palsy
content: Step 1: ENT or neurology referral for all new-onset facial nerve palsies to establish cause.
Step 2: Neuroimaging for all recurrent facial nerve palsy to exclude inflammatory or neoplastic causes.
Step 3: Immediate ocular surface protection with lubricants (preservative-free tears day/ointment night).
Step 4: Assess need for lid closure (taping at night or temporary tarsorrhaphy).

sections.title: Surgical & Chronic Management
content: Insertion of gold weights to the upper lid for chronic cases.
Late surgical options: Facial nerve repair.
Late surgical options: Nerve substitution.
Late surgical options: Muscle transposition.
Crocodile tears (gustatory hyperlacrimation 2° aberrant regeneration): Transcutaneous injection of botulinum toxin to the lacrimal gland.

sections.title: CRITICAL WARNINGS
content: Do not automatically assume every palsy is Bell's Palsy.
Blinding exposure keratopathy risk is high.
Recurrent palsy requires neuroimaging to exclude neoplastic causes.
Anti-herpes simplex antivirals alone confer no recovery benefit compared to placebo.
